newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Recognition on cards for Afghanistan's Taleban.
newsitem.headline: Recognition on cards for Afghanistan's Taleban.

text.p: Sweeping northern victories by the Taleban militia and its allies leave reluctant neighbours and the United Nations no real choice but to follow Pakistan's lead and recognise it as the government of Afghanistan, analysts said on Sunday.

Iran, Turkey, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and other regional states held back from acknowledging Taleban when the purist Islamic movement captured the capital Kabul last September and fanned out to control two-thirds of the country.

Even Pakistan, which was on friendly terms with the new rulers, had --until now -- withheld formal recognition, denying accusations that it was taking sides in the war next door or arming a movement that sprang up among young refugees in Pakistani camps.

But anti-Taleban forces in northern Afghanistan have now collapsed with startling speed. Uzbek General Abdul Rashid Dostum fled abroad over the weekend, leaving the opposition alliance he had led controlling less than 10 percent of the country.

Pakistan's formal diplomatic recognition was announced by Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan on Sunday and analysts say other neighbours can hardly deny that the Taleban has almost total control in a country which has not known peace and unity for nearly 20 years.

"I think it will become very, very difficult not to recognise the reality on the ground," Samina Ahmed, of Islamabad's Institute of Regional Studies think tank, told Reuters before the Pakistani announcement.

"But on the other hand it's going to be equally difficult to say that we recognise the Taleban without Taleban conceding a certain degree of autonomy and representation to others within Kabul," she said.
She said the mainly ethnic Pashtun Taleban would have to ensure that their alliances with local commanders were seen to involve all communities.

The Pakistani foreign minister told reporters that the Taleban government was now "in effective control of most of the territory of Afghanistan and is representative of all ethnic groups in that country."
Another analyst, who asked not be identified, said there was no way for regional states to disregard the Taleban.

"They will have to accept because they do not have any other option," he said. "If the entire country is under the control of one group, how can anyone else challenge that, not even the United Nations," the analyst added.

Agha Murtaza Pooya, head of the Institute of Strategic Studies in Islamabad, said the Taleban's success and its consolidation was not surprising because the militia had been working on it over the last few months.
"Dostum was bound to collapse in any case. He was not a very good factor in the unity of Afghanistan," Pooya said.
He said it would be easy for the Taleban now to establish its writ in the country and that should lead to its recognition by the Central Asian states and other neighbours.

"There was a slight apprehension, often expressed by Iran, but the Iranians in the last two or three months have improved their level of communication and interaction with Taleban," Pooya said. "So their apprehensions have been either allayed or they have sort of answered.

"As far as the Uzbeks or Tajiks and others are concerned, I think no matter who has what apprehensions, as long as the Taleban are supported by the people, nobody has really a right to object," he said.
He said even the United Nations, where the ousted government occupies the Afghan seat, should not try to bring about a government that does not match the wishes of the Afghan people.

Afghanistan holds the key to trade between the energy-rich states of central Asia and the Indian sub-continent. Good relations with Afghanistan's new rulers will be vital to fully exploit their resources.
